provenance: The Collection of Nina and Gordon Bunshaft, New York. | The Museum of Modern Art, New York. | Sale: Christie's New York, Contemporary Art (Part II), May 4, 1995, Lot 147. | Acquired from the above by the present owner. | | Literature | M. Loreau, Catalogue des travaux de Jean Dubuffet, Fascicule XXV: Arbres, murs, architectures, Paris, 1974, no. 118 (illustrated p. 117). | | | | Belonging to Dubuffet's L'Hourloupe cycle, one of his most celebrated passages of work that occupied him from 1962 to 1974 and extended his graphic language into the realm of sculpture and architecture, Promeneuse et Promeneur is an exceptionally elegant and rare example of the artist's sculptural foray. The subjects of the present work, outlined in the distinctive black tracery against a paper-white ground, appear as drawings conjured into being. In Promeneuse et Promeneur, Dubuffet has translated the spontaneity of his drawn line into three-dimensional form. This transformation, from the mental to the material, embodies the central premise of L'Hourloupe and indeed much of Dubuffet's lifelong concern: that art could give form to thought itself, imagining a novel universe of forms and meaning. | | Formerly in the collection of Nina and Gordon Bunshaft, patrons of some of the most renowned artists of the twentieth century, one need only consider a small number of the artworks the Bunshafts gifted to the Museum of Modern Art, New York, by bequest in 1995, to appreciate their profound connoisseurship and impact on the MoMA collection itself: Helen Frankenthaler's Chairman of the Board (1971); Alberto Giacometti's Tall Figure III (1960); Fernand Léger's The Mirror (1925); Jean Dubuffet's Facades d'immeubles (1946); Henry Moore's Animal Form (1969-1970); Joan Miro's Moonbird (1966). | | In the intimacy of this tabletop sculpture, we glimpse not only Dubuffet mastering a wonderfully concise scale, but the friendship and patronage through which it emerged. Bunshaft, longtime architect of Skidmore, Owings & Merril and winner of the Pritzker Architecture Prize in 1988, was not known to be affable or talkative. It's been noted by biographer Nicholas Adams, however, that his friendships with artists revealed a softer, more vulnerable side to the terse architect. In a 1972 letter to Dubuffet, written after the unveiling of Groupe de quatre arbres – a commission for the plaza of the Chase Manhattan skyscraper Bunshaft had designed and opened in 1961 – Bunshaft reflected: "I enjoyed your visit here tremendously. I felt that although I have known you, off and on, for many years, this is the first time we really became closer" (quoted in: Nicholas Adams, "Silence and Gordon Bunshaft," Yale University Press, November 19, 2019, Online). This sentiment reveals the closeness of spirit between two creators who had each contributed their vision to 28 Liberty Street. | | After long-term ownership since the sale from the MoMA-Bunshaft bequest in 1995, the opportunity to now acquire a museum-quality L'Hourloupe sculpture by Jean Dubuffet steeped in history is not to be missed.

provenance: Wendell & Esther Wilcox Collection, Chapel Hill, North Carolina (acquired directly from the artist). | Acquired from the above by the present owner. | | Exhibited | New York, Karma Gallery, Gertrude Abercrombie, August 9 - September 23, 2018. | | Literature | The artist's handlist, Paintings 1950-1959, no. 11. | | | Small Phonograph, painted in 1955, offers a sparse vignette of highly personal iconography. While deceptively straightforward, the work is imbued with a quietly powerful dynamism capable of transforming the mundane everyday into the extraordinary. Gertrude Abercrombie's distinctive visual language was heavily informed by the innermost depths of her subconscious, dreams, and lived experiences. Drawing inspiration from the "simple things that are a little strange," Abercrombie's painted realm of magical realism allowed her to question one's existence as traditionally understood, while also creating an alternate reality (Abercrombie quoted in University of Illinois Exhibitions of Contemporary American Painting, 1951, p. 157). | | Small Phonograph is the last of three known examples that Abercrombie painted of this subject between the years of 1954 and 1955. The present work's iconography and composition are nearly identical to that of Inheritance (1955). Measuring in at 48 x 32 inches, Small Phonograph's direct antecedent captures the prosaic nature of the exact tableau on a larger scale. Small Phonograph was created with the intent to duplicate the larger Inheritance, which was sold to Dwayne Andreas for $1,000. Andreas, who was to become the enormously influential CEO of Archer Daniels Midland, likely paid Abercrombie the largest sum the artist had ever received for a painting in her lifetime. | | As is characteristic of Abercrombie's oeuvre, the present work's compositional space is not overly complicated. Every element contributes to the structure of the composition, endowing an essential significance to each motif carefully placed within the interior scene. Abercrombie's mastery of the still life genre shines in Small Phonograph. The beautifully rendered perspective of the phonograph, careful chiaroscuro of the speaker, crisp drapery of the tablecloth, and carefully curated placement of objects in relation to one another evoke a sense of quiet mystery that sparks the viewer's interest. | | The phonograph, ornate claw-foot table, and Edison cylinder box were personal possessions of Abercrombie's and were often used as objects within her work. The antique table is particularly distinctive and frequently appeared in Abercrombie's paintings beginning in the early 1940s. More than just an object observed in her home, the phonograph motif is emblematic of various associations that strike chords of deep personal significance for the artist. Raised by opera singer parents, Gertrude Abercrombie was immersed within the world of music from an early age. Her marriage to music critic and record shop owner Frank Sandiford resulted in scores of introductions to jazz musicians, many of which would become lasting friendships. Referred to by many as the 'jazz witch', Abercrombie was a radiant beam of light within the Chicago arts scene, and continued to host countless parties and performances with musicians from the jazz world long after her divorce from Sandiford. During an era when black musicians were often banned from many hotels, Abercrombie's home became a refuge for the likes of Charlie Parker and Dizzy Gillespie, a salon of sorts in which the phonograph would have functioned as the touchstone. | | The phonograph's dainty gold chain holds the speaker in position against the buttressing vertical support, creating a pointed, triangular shape reminiscent of a witch's hat. Once remarking that: "it is always myself that I paint," Gertrude Abercrombie liked to represent herself in various guises, and most heavily associated herself with the witch. Through her identification as a witch, Abercrombie was able to embrace the complexity of selfhood, gaining a sense of agency within her painted worlds that she grappled with in real life. As a result, imagery of witchcraft and sorcery is prevalent throughout her work: the inclusion of cats, broomsticks, and pointed hats acting as the artist's talismans. As such, this simple still life reverberates with some of the pivotal themes of Abercrombie's life: the sturdy table with its personal, historical references (which may also have been a piece of furniture she grew up with), the role of music in the lives of her family and herself, and the allusion to her own power in the role of the witch. | | Small Phonograph was first acquired directly from the artist by Wendell Wilcox, the American novelist and story writer who remained one of Abercrombie's closest, most important friends throughout her life. Upon Wilcox's death, the work was thence acquired by August Becker, a fellow Chicago-based artist and dear friend of both Wendell and Gertrude. Having remained in the collection of August Becker, the present work carries an emblematic significance that harkens directly back to the artist, and the vibrant milieu of arts and culture she surrounded herself with. With references to Abercrombie's past and present, allusions to music and witches, Small Phonograph comes to auction for the first time as a beautiful example of the fantastical sense of mystery that Abercombie conjured through a deft hand and meticulous execution. A work whose meaning goes beyond the unassuming imagery of an old phonograph, generating the enigma, poignancy, and magic that are now so heavily ensconced within the interpretations of Abercrombie's work.

provenance: Private collection, California. | Thence by descent to the present owner. | | | | In the late 1950s, California-born artist Miyoko Ito began developing an impressive dexterity with oil painting while retaining the sensibilities of her education in the Berkeley School of Watercolor. This went hand in hand with the evolution of her unique take on organic abstraction, characterized by long, tubular and ovoid forms undulating in fields of earthy hues. The titles of her paintings during this period, including the present lot entitled The Sea, refer back to the natural and physical world, but the works themselves make no literal representations. Instead, her strength and precision in evoking a certain energy or mood without any reliance on figurative representation emerges. Deeply inspired by the work of Pierre Bonnard, Ito adopted his technique of underpainting in red and cool tones, with which she conveyed a sense of intentionality and intrinsic harmony in her use of color. Beyond just technical influence, there are echoes of Bonnard's slender-limbed nudes and tightly packed, flattened interiors in The Sea. | | The solid patches of deep colors, delineated by hard edges of this period gradually gave way to delicate gradients and more variable spatial dimensionality. Through further experimentation along the boundaries of abstraction, Ito entered the subsequent era of her work for which she is best known. The warm glowing palettes and vaguely architectural, liminal environments she constructed in this later era of her career are highly regarded as her finest work. The mystery and magic of her mature work also subtly reveal the impact of Surrealism, which Ito inevitably gleaned from her peers during the 1960s in Chicago. | | When asked in a 1978 interview whether, as a student, she tried to emulate the work of such giants of the canon, Ito explained that "Picasso and Cezanne gave [her] understanding" ("Oral History Interview With Myoko Ito at The Oxbow Summer School Of Painting, Saugatuck, Michigan, July 20, 1978", Archives of American Art, Smithsonian Institution, Online). This attitude is illustrative of her singular approach to artmaking and the conviction in her vision. Her work reflects a diverse education, from her early schooling in Japan, to her formative years in Berkeley and later the School of Art Institute of Chicago. For Ito, painting was a way of life that carried her through one upheaval after the other, beginning with the nervous breakdown she suffered as a child in Yokohama followed by her experience of the Japanese American internment in the United States during World War II. Miyoko Ito: Heart of Hearts, the first major monograph dedicated to Ito's life and work was published in 2024 by Pre-Echo Press and Jordan Stein. And despite her untimely death over 40 years ago, international acclaim for the artist is greater than ever.

provenance: Ankrum Gallery, Los Angeles. | Acquired from the above by the present owner in 1972. | | Exhibited | Oakland, Oakland Museum of California, Black Untitled II: Dimensions of the Figure, November 2 - December 12, 1971. | Los Angeles, Ankrum Gallery, Suzanne Jackson: Paintings and Drawings, September 1972, no. 40. | | Literature | S. Jackson, What I Love: Paintings, Poetry, and a Drawing, Los Angeles, 1972 (illustrated p. 6). | | | | A gem of the artist's self-dubbed "romantic period," Muntu in My Garden by Suzanne Jackson returns to the public stage for the first time since its debut at Ankrum Gallery in Los Angeles in 1972. The title of Jackson's ongoing retrospective at the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art poses the question, What is Love? Love is at the very core of Suzanne Jackson's practice; nowhere is this more evident than in the present lot. | | This quintessential example of her early 1970s work is characterized by delicate and mesmerizing colors, applied by meticulously layering thin washes of acrylic paint – a signature technique Jackson still uses today on her less conventional "anti-canvases." At the center of Muntu in My Garden, a heart-shaped being peers at the viewer through barely open eyes exuding calm and sagacity. A faintly blue-green tree emerges from the central figure's heart-shaped face, the blue hues trickling from the tree down to the heart's face – they are inextricably linked in symbiosis. Overhead, a jewel-toned bird descends from the trees with its beak slightly opened as if to emit a call or song. Grasping hands sprout from the bottom of the canvas, some veiled in layers of gesso among a lone red rose. Suspended in a milky dreamscape, these motifs come together in an expression of the alchemical power which runs through all living things. Where Jackson introduces the human figure, it is typically in a hybrid or metamorphic stage; through these visual metaphors, she illustrates the link between flora and fauna, human and earth, life and fantasy. Since her childhood in Fairbanks, Alaska, Jackson developed a reverence for the natural world that continues to inspire her work today. | | Returning to the central heart-shaped face, Jackson selected this striking motif for the cover of What I Love, her 1972 book illustrating recent paintings, poetry, and drawings. The book also reads as a catalogue of her 1972 solo show at Ankrum Gallery which included Muntu in My Garden among an extraordinary suite of early 1970s paintings, many of which are now held by notable institutions and private collections. While briefly residing in Los Angeles, NBA legend Bill Russell acquired Jackson's There is Something Between Us from the very same show. The NFL athlete and actor-turned-artist Bernie Casey was not only also represented by Ankrum, but a prominent supporter of Jackson's own artist-run Gallery 32 and a mutual friend of Russell and Jackson. Another powerful work in the 1972 show, Nest, was initially in the collection of Ben Hazard, the first Black curator of the Oakland Museum of Art; in 2024 the work was acquired by the Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA). During Hazard's successful tenure as Curator, Special Exhibitions and Education, the Oakland Museum of Art included both Muntu in My Garden and There is Something Between Us in a group exhibition entitled Black Untitled II: Dimensions of the Figure. | | Even more than a gallery in the commercial sense of the word, Gallery 32, which Jackson organized, financed and operated from 1968-1970 in Los Angeles, brought together a community of artists who were otherwise given few opportunities to show their work, especially Jackson's fellow Black artists. A circle of artists including Senga Nengudi, Betye Saar, David Hammons, and Timothy Washington among others brought the space to life with creative experimentation and critical discussion, which was vital in the post-Watts Rebellion era when most White-owned galleries still refused to show Black artists. During this time, Jackson was also actively involved with the Black Arts Council, an organization that successfully lobbied LACMA and its board to include the work of Black artists in the museum's programming. | | Suzanne Jackson's career of over six decades has taken her across the country and around the world. Today she is based between Savannah, Georgia, which has been her home since 1996, and St. Remy, New York. Her artistic practice spans a plethora of mediums including, but not limited to, painting, drawing, poetry, installation, dance and theater. While her recent three-dimensional paintings incorporating found objects, fabric scraps, repurposed plastic and other detritus look quite different at first glance from her ethereal 1970s compositions, the same guiding principles remain: love, beauty and peace. | | Jackson is the subject of a traveling retrospective currently on view at SFMOMA and has recently been featured in exhibitions at the WIELS Contemporary Art Centre, Brussels; the Whitney Museum of American Art, New York; Goldsmith's Center for Contemporary Art, London; The Museum of Modern Art, New York; and the Galleria d'Arte Moderna of Milan. Her work is held by a rapidly growing list of institutional collections including LACMA; MoMA, New York; SFMOMA; Whitney Museum of American Art, New York; Buffalo AKG Art Museum; MCA San Diego; California African American Museum, Los Angeles; The Walker Art Center, Minneapolis; Baltimore Museum of Art; the Art Institute of Chicago; and The Morgan Library and Museum, New York.

provenance: The Collection of Timothy Egert, Maryland (acquired by 1991). | | Literature | The Martin Wong Foundation, Martin Wong Catalogue Raisonné, online (illustrated). | | | A towering edifice that rises toward golden skies of wingless skaters resembling the Putti of Giotto's frescoes, Martin Wong's Houston Street & Avenue B is a triumph of his late painting. Filled with allegory and personal inflection, this recently rediscovered work boasts an abundance of motifs and symbols that speak to Wong's centrality in the Downtown scene of the 1980s and 1990s, his Graffiti collaborators, the architecture of the Lower East Side, and his tapestried heritage. From his late lover Miguel Piñero, pictured at its base, to the stern, masonry visage of Lady Liberty, Houston Street & Avenue B paints a story of love and death, freedom and detention, New York City and the American Dream. Few artists of the Postmodern period have achieved such poetry and sincerity; fewer still have come to represent an authentic voice in such pivotal decades. Whilst Jean-Michel Basquiat synthesized abstraction, Graffiti and the energy of the Downtown scene to the toast of art world royalty, Martin Wong took no liberties in illustrating the same milieu with lucidity, ambition, and painterly prowess. | | A third-generation Chinese-American, Wong was raised in the Chinatown district of San Francisco, becoming an active member of the Bay Area art scene. After college, he worked as a performance artist and portraitist, later journeying across Asia, collecting and selling the antiques amassed throughout his travels. By the late 1970s, Wong's creative output had turned exclusively to painting, and, in 1978, he found himself in New York, inescapably drawn to the city's gritty, wild and vivid atmosphere. Moving from the desolate, foggy shores of Northern California to the allure of Manhattan, Wong found inspiration in the firefighters, b-boys and skateboarders running the city. This was Wong's new life, one where he "dressed like a rodeo cowboy and ran with graffiti artists who were tagging the neighborhood" (H. Cotter, "Martin Wong, an Urban Visionary With a Hungry Eye," The New York Times, November 19, 2015, Online). | | Upon his arrival in New York, Wong found and rented an empty apartment at 141 Ridge Street from 1982 to 1994, settling himself in the heart of the Lower East Side. Graffiti lined the entryway, mirroring the landscape of his new neighborhood. The apartment, a 1920s tenement building, engulfed the artist in a sea of brick, the view from his room that of a similarly faced building, covered in crumbling red bricks and lined with identically sized windows. It was within this apartment, and the decrepit motel room the artist inhabited beforehand, that Wong first incorporated bricks into his paintings, imagery that would become a central motif within his artistic oeuvre. Wong understood the materiality of the city, having graduated years before with a degree in ceramics. He used the bare brick walls of the surrounding buildings as his subject matter, a single object functioning as a metaphor for the urban landscape, embodying themes of spatial containment and psychological entrapment. | | It is just four blocks from Wong's Ridge Street apartment that Houston Street & Avenue B takes its title. Amid a bustling intersection at the very bottom of Alphabet City, Houston Street & Avenue B features a tall chain linked fence topped with swaths of barbed wire and a fiery golden sky dotted with skateboard riding figures. In the foreground stands Miguel Piñero, a poet and playwright, and Wong's longtime creative and romantic partner. Hair held back by a striped cap, Piñero tilts his head back, gulping down the contents of a dark bottle. The entirety of this scene unfolds against a backdrop of brick, swirling together to form the face of the Statue of Liberty, a symbolic source of inspiration for artists since her unveiling in 1886. | | For Wong, the Statue of Liberty was one of his most potent, recurring motifs. If Lady Liberty was once the emblem of the nation's ideal of freedom – and of welcome to those émigrés deboarding at Ellis Island in the preceding century – Wong recasts it here as the fortress of exclusion. His characters nonetheless transcend the architecture of control. In this sense, Houston Street & Avenue B articulates an alternative American sublime, one measured not by monumental progress but by the ascendence of those who move through its ruins. | | | A Lower Eastside Poem (excerpt) | Miguel Piñero | | Just once before I die | I want to climb up on | a tenement sky | to dream my lungs out till | I cry | then scatter my ashes thru | the Lower East Side. | | So let me sing my song tonight | let me feel out of sight | and let all eyes be dry | when they scatter my ashes thru | the Lower East Side. | | | The Lower East side of the 1980s, known as Loisaida by its black and Latino residents, attracted swarms of artists with its gritty charm. A vibrant, defiant community, immersed in the sounds of hardcore, punk, and hip hop. With bands like The Clash, the Misfits, and the Beastie Boys as its soundtrack, the Lower East Side stood in stark opposition to the rising tide of Reagan-era gentrification, becoming a sanctuary for outcasts and a powerful space for self-expression. Wong drew inspiration from these very sources to craft works that were passionate, poetic, and precisely executed, defying conventional expectations around ethnicity, culture, and sexuality. | | A remarkable and visionary artist of the late 20th Century, one who represents the authentic voice of the New York new wave, Martin Wong's work can be found in the permanent collections of the Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York; the Whitney Museum of American Art, New York; the Art Institute of Chicago; the de Young Museum, Los Angeles; the Museum of Modern Art, New York; and the New York Historical Society. Retrospectives of his work took place at New York's New Museum in 1998 and the Bronx Museum, New York, in 2015. | | Rediscovered after decades in private hands, the painting stands today as one of Wong's most profound meditations on the paradoxes of freedom. It transforms the vernacular of downtown life into a lasting parable of hope, mourning, and transcendence; a monument not to power, but to the poetry of survival.

Rabinow (eds.), The Steins Collect, Matisse, Picasso and the Parisian Avant-Garde, exh. cat., San Francisco Museum of Art, San Francisco, 2011, no. 99 (illustrated pp. 386 & 408). | | | La femme aux cheveux noirs, painted circa 1901, hails from a crucial moment in the artistic career of a founding father of modern art. Created on the cusp of his radical and defining Fauve epoch, the work's layered brushwork, bold delineation, and Cezanne-esque tonal construction offer the viewer a rare glimpse into Matisse's earliest development as a modern artist, rejecting the academic formalities of an anachronistic turn-of-the-century Europe. Contrary to the brazen Fauve canvases Matisse would first exhibit in 1905, the initially austere palette and direct, confrontational gaze of La femme aux cheveux noirs is a striking exemplar of the artist's early portraiture. While the reserved nudes, greys, and black hues of La femme aux cheveux noirs are present, we see the subtle foreshadowing to the later Fauvist style weaved within; flecks of blue on the collarbone, a richness to the pinks, bright greens and yellows developing as one's gaze lengthens. This delicate variation offering a clear visual trajectory in the artist's development towards 'pure color'. | | In the early 1900s, Matisse was a struggling, relatively unknown artist. According to fellow artist Maurice Boudot-Lamotte, he even reportedly accepted five francs from the owner of a junk-stall on Boulevard Raspail for three of his paintings. In dire financial straits and with a family to consider, Matisse felt caught between his intrinsic need to push the boundaries of traditional representation, and the obligation to appease collectors and generate revenue to support his family. It was during this time that Matisse began to explore different ways of rendering the world around him. The present work presciently anticipates some of the most radical, iconic aspects of his oeuvre, such as the intensity and concentration of color in his Fauve pictures, manifested here in the emphatically worked flesh and assured sense of line. | | The sitter's graceful visage is formed through thick, lavish brushstrokes applied with a heavy impasto, creating a strong delineation of subject and background, and a powerfully expressive contrast of a subtle multitude of colors that creates the impression of space opening in depth. Rare in its intimate scale and stark background, the black tonal contrast enhances the chromatic effervescence of the sitter's bare skin and offers an intimate study of great psychological power. Whilst completed earlier than Amedeo Modigliani's iconic nudes and portraiture of the 1910s, there is a handling, emotion, and expression in La femme aux cheveux noirs that forces a comparison and possible influence between the artists at this pivotal juncture. | | Before 1900, Matisse had produced very few figural studies. Following his renewed interest in the human form, however, portraiture became a renowned fixture throughout his prolific oeuvre. He wrote in 1908: "What interests me most is neither still life nor landscape, but the human figure. It is that which best permits me to express my so-to-speak religious attitude toward life" (H. Matisse, 'Notes of a Painter', in La Grande Review, December 25, 1908). In the present work, Matisse depicts his subject with an honest simplicity, forgoing anatomical exactitude and identifying details in favor of capturing the essential qualities that: "suggest the deep gravity which persists in every human being [...] Expression, for me, does not reside in passions flaring up in a human face or manifested by violent movement. The entire arrangement of my picture is expressive . . ." (ibid). Here, the jutting prow of the figure's collarbone and shoulders commands space within the composition, while the rest of her body contorts and almost recedes into the background of the canvas. | | Whilst the exact identity of the sitter of La femme aux cheveux noirs is unknown, records of correspondence in 1970 between Margaret Potter, Associate Curator at the Museum of Modern Art, and the family of the present owners revealed that Matisse's daughter, Marguerite Duthuit Faure, confirmed the sitter was a model frequently used by Matisse at the time. Rarely working from his imagination, the burgeoning artist hired countless models for periods both long and short throughout his career, often with the sitters themselves becoming iconic within modern canon. Matisse preferred paid models to sitters or patrons because he thought them to be much more malleable, offering him more artistic freedom and experimentation. As a paid 'employee', his models' identity and characterization could be manipulated in service of his artistic needs, whereas with portraits for patrons, friends, and family, he often felt beholden to preserve their individuality and remain accountable to social or professional interdependence. As such, the figure in the present work is rendered with generalized features that maintain little individuality: capturing the model's innate being is not the primary object of Matisse's representation, it is an experiment of medium and feeling. | | When referring to the model in La femme aux cheveux noirs, Duthuit also noted the use of the very same model in 1900 for a sculpture entitled Buste Ancien. Given the distinctive pictorial composition, and its relation to Buste Ancien, the present work was most likely realized in conjunction with a group of sculptural studies Matisse created between 1900 and 1903. As he began to create figural studies with greater frequency, he became preoccupied with the challenge of rendering a figure's arms in a manner so as to avoid interference with the silhouette of the torso. Ever the innovator, Matisse would often experiment with other mediums as a means of working through pictorial challenges that emerged in his painting. As such, there are numerous sculptures, paintings, and drawings from the turn of the century through which he experimented with different contrapposto stances, and the subsequent effect this had on the figure's torso and upper chest. | | An important and rare example of Matisse's Pre-Fauvist work, La femme aux cheveux noirs is also distinguished by its exceptional provenance. Purchased in Paris in 1909, this work remained in the personal collection of Sarah and Michael Stein for decades. These American collectors would arguably go on to become some of Matisse's most important patrons and promoters. In 1903 when Michael Stein and his wife Sarah moved to Paris from San Francisco, at the urging of his siblings Leo and Gertrude Stein, they swiftly immersed themselves within the cultural and social milieu of the Parisian avant-garde. As with Michael's siblings, this meant filling their 58 rue Madame apartment with their latest acquisitions; generally all exquisite examples of modern art. While Michael and Sarah's early collection included the names of Cézanne, Renoir, and Picasso, from 1905 it was soon to be dominated by the striking work of Henri Matisse. In a circa 1911-1914 photograph, taken in the apartment, La femme aux cheveux noirs can be seen on the wall behind the seated Sarah Stein and her friend, alongside a sculpture of the same model. | | The apartment, now filled with Matisse paintings, was the setting for an open house every Saturday evening, and their salon of modern art soon became the fashionable gathering place for connoisseurs and dilettantes alike. For most who attended Sarah and Michael's weekend salons, the work of Matisse would have been unfamiliar, and, to some, even savagely offensive. Slowly but surely, however, those who entered the Stein's apartment, mesmerized by Sarah's intelligence and eloquence, began to begrudgingly accept Matisse as the brilliant artist he was. Recounting his many nights spent as a guest at the Stein's, famed art dealer Ambroise Vollard wrote: "beautifully gowned in original costumes, antique jewelry... Sarah sat on the couch in the corner explaining to everybody the greatness of Matisse. People listened to her, unconvinced, but overwhelmed by her enthusiasm and authority" (Vollard, Recollections of a Picture Dealer, London, 1936, p. 137). Frequently taking their Matisse paintings back with them to show friends in America, Michael and Sarah Stein played a pivotal role in promoting Matisse's art within the United States, and are often lauded with carrying the artist's name outside of France. | | In addition to patron, Matisse also came to view Sarah Stein as a close confidante and friend. According to Therese Jelenko, friend and frequent guest of the Stein's, Matisse would regularly come to the Rue Madame carrying bundles of his pictures, and Sarah would: "tell him what she thought of things, sometimes rather bluntly. He'd seem to always listen and always argue about it" (ibid). Annette Rosenshine further recounted that: "I recall seeing Matisse in the Steins' apartment when he was in the throes of struggling with a new creative expression. There he found solace in unburdening his latest problems and uncertainties to Sarah Stein, knowing that he would receive sensitive, sympathetic understanding. The talk and friendship were valuable to him" (A. Rosenshine, Life's Not a Paragraph). Matisse valued Sarah's opinion and would often seek out her guidance when met with a particularly difficult artistic problem, once stating that: "she (Sarah) knows more about my paintings than I do" (Matisse quoted in Pollack, The Collectors: Dr. Claribel and Miss Etta Cone, New York, 1962, p. 270). | | The Stein's collection of Matisse works, while vast in size and breadth, is particularly notable for the way in which it acutely captured the artist's creative spirit. As one of the last Matisse works the Steins would buy due to limited space and the artist's steadily increasing prices, La femme aux cheveux noirs' inclusion in such a prominent collection speaks to the work's emblematic significance amongst Matisse's tremendous and coveted artistic output. | | Acquired by Michael and Sarah Stein at its last presentation at auction over a century ago, La femme aux cheveux noirs was later included in the seminal 1970 exhibition at the Museum of Modern Art that sought to regather the exceptional collections of this trailblazing family of collectors. Returning to auction with a history and pedigree only the finest works can boast, the present work remains a preeminent testament to a key artist-patron relationship in art history - a seminal masterpiece.

Mesens (ed.), London Bulletin, no. 4-5, July 1938 (illustrated p. 30). | P. Matisse & K. Sage (eds.), Yves Tanguy, Un Recueil de ses oeuvres, New York, 1963, no. 218 (illustrated p. 108). | P. Waldberg, Yves Tanguy, Brussels, 1977 (illustrated p. 85). | L. Riou, Ma vie blanche et noire, Notes sur Yves Tanguy, Baye, 1996, pp. 10 & 28. | | | "Yves Tanguy, the painter of terrible aerial, subterranean, and maritime elegances, the man in whom I see the moral adornment of our time: my adorable friend" | | - Andre Breton, 'Yves Tanguy', in London Bulletin alongside an illustration of the present work, no. 4-5, London, July 1938, p. 32). | | Though Yves Tanguy received no formal artistic training, his meticulous draftsmanship and inventive vision resulted in a highly refined, iconic personal style that transformed the boundaries of Modernist painting and helped to establish Surrealism as a major artistic movement. Bridging the gap between abstraction and figuration, landscape and still-life, Surrealist dreamscape and automatic form, Yves Tanguy's utterly unique artistry came to epitomize the surrealist movement and has inspired generations. | | While surrounded by the arts, literature, and culture from an early age, it wasn't until 1923, when passing a Giorgio de Chirico painting in the windows of Paul Guillaume's gallery, that Yves Tanguy decided that he, too, would become a painter. Struck by the enigmatic, metaphysical imagery of de Chirico's painting, Tanguy soon became interested in the Surrealist movement and was introduced to André Breton, the movement's protagonist and founding leader, in 1925. By 1926, the June issue of La Révolution surréaliste had featured a reproduction of Tanguy's early work, resulting in his recognition as an 'official' Surrealist artist. In the following year of 1927, Tanguy's mature style developed with an astonishing abruptness, and he exhibited his first one-man show at the Galerie Surréaliste in Paris. It is in this mature style that Tanguy's iconic dreamscapes of amorphous forms, as seen in the present work, emerge. | | This new, highly personal pictorial language was heavily influenced by the childhood summers Tanguy spent off the coast of Brittany, France. The prehistoric rock formations observed by Tanguy in his youth would later be subconsciously reimagined into the nebulous forms that occupy the sparse, vast expanses of his painted 'inscapes' of the mind. The haunting imagery of Tanguy's work, like so many of the Surrealists', was also heavily informed by the rubble, dilapidated ruins, and barren towns Tanguy encountered while growing up in WWI-era France. Equally important was his trip to North Africa in 1930, where he observed natural geological structures and stratifications, which were to appear as abstracted motifs in his paintings. While Tanguy felt deeply inspired by the work of de Chirico and also influenced by Hieronymus Bosch's mythical imagery, he seldom discussed personal influences from his private life that informed the imagery within his own works. | | Painted in 1938, Je tourne la tête vers moi (I Turn My Head Toward Myself) encapsulates a pivotal time in both Tanguy's art and life. As tensions began to escalate across Europe and the world, Tanguy was the first Surrealist artist to flee Europe for America in November of 1939, marking 1938 as what was to be his last year in the City of Light. His final years in Paris proved to be a time of great artistic development for Tanguy, as he worked towards achieving a completely ambiguous, horizonless space. This new pictorial development in the artist's mature work called for an intuitive, largely subliminal approach to painting, further cementing his works as a wholly unique, sacred poetry of the inner mind. Writing in admiration of this new-found, meditative approach to Tanguy's work, André Breton lauded that: | | "There are no landscapes. There is not even a horizon [...] There is only, physically speaking, our immense suspicion which surrounds everything [...] Where most observers would see only a favourite setting for obscure and magnificent metamorphoses, there is actually presented the first survey – achieved without the aid of legends – of a considerable extent of the mental world which is not in its Genesis" (A. Breton, 'At an Equal Distance', in Yves Tanguy par André Breton, New York, 1946). | | The rich swaths of hazy greys and modulating hues of blue present in Je tourne la tête vers moi form an ambivalent fusion of land into sky, an enigmatic vista of the mind in which space is both continuous and fluidly ephemeral. Upon first delineating this vast, weightless landscape of blue and grey swells, Tanguy would instinctively begin to populate the composition with spontaneously generated forms. Each new motif suggested its subsequent counterpart, until a dreamscape of delicate equilibrium became fully realized, each element held in place by a mysterious force of internal gravity. | | Tanguy found it most freeing when he relied solely on intuition and creative imagination, noting that: "I found that if I planned a picture beforehand, it never surprised me, and surprises are pleasure in painting" (Tanguy quoted in Yves Tanguy, exh. cat. New York, 1955, p. 17). When reflecting on his creative process shortly before his premature death in 1955, Yves Tanguy insisted that the "element of surprise in the creation of a work of art is, for me, the most important thing" (Y. Tanguy, 'The Creative Process', in Art Digest, Vol. 28, no. 8, New York, January 1954, p. 14). His unique worlds, while subconsciously conjured, were not, however, automatically articulated like the scribbled 'automatic drawings' of his Surrealist colleagues. Neatness and precision were deeply ingrained attributes of Tanguy's mind and personality, and he infused his surreal visions with an ultra-precise realism. Je tourne la tête vers moi offers viewers a curious glimpse into the dichotomous nature of Tanguy's surreal dreamworld, conjured through a scrupulous technique of hyper-realism. As a result of Tanguy's reverential attention to detail, the present work's array of nebulous forms punctuate the hazy, modulated backdrop with stunning sense of alacrity. Cacti-like forms and geometric structures resembling the scientific model of a module are interconnected through a constellation of taut, gossamer-like threads that stretch into the composition's deep perspective. The present work's amalgamation of disparate, elemental forms and innate sensations conjures the enigmatic inner world of Yves Tanguy's creative genius and presents a primitive, yet unprecedented version of reality- a hallucinatory myth of his time. | | Tanguy's intimate psychological landscapes, infused with an inscrutable mystery that is fully realized in the present work, were extolled by front-runners of the Surrealist movement, Andre Breton and the Belgian artist-turned-publisher E.L.T. Mesens. Je tourne la tête vers moi is one of only three illustrated paintings by Tanguy in the April 1938 edition of the London Bulletin, the highly influential Surrealist periodical Mesens edited and published, perfectly illustrating the high regard it was held in by Tanguy's contemporaries. Alongside this illustration, the London Bulletin included two texts by André Breton and Paul Eluard, commending the artist and his influence on surrealism. The present work was subsequently exhibited in the corresponding 1938 Tanguy Exhibition at the Guggenheim Jeune Gallery on 30 Cork Street on an hors-catalogue basis – possibly due to its only recent creation. Whilst not listed in the exhibition guide, this inclusion was confirmed by the artist's wife, Kay Sage, in a letter to the San Franciscan owners in 1957. Leaving for the United States after the London exhibition, yet not included in Pierre Matisse Gallery's October 1939 Tanguy show organized by Sage, it was only after Charlotte Mack, friend of the family and one of the original owners of Kandinsky's Lila (Lot 10A), notified the artist's wife of the location of Je tourne la tête vers moi, that anyone knew of its whereabouts in the US. This resulted in an intimate series of correspondence between the artist's wife and the family, ultimately reuniting her with the piece and ensuring it was included in the vital Tanguy literature, published in 1963. | | The acquisition of the work from California-based Stendahl Galleries, circa 1949-1950, by the family demonstrated a clairvoyant appreciation for the bold, cutting-edge output of the French modernists. Privately selling Je tourne la tête vers moi for a brief time in the 1970s, only to buy the work back in 1980 after finding it impossible to live without, demonstrates the true appreciation the owners had for this stunning painting on an art historical level and, more importantly, a deeply sentimental one. | | A scrupulous, reverential craftsman working in his spotless studio, Tanguy only painted when the spirit moved him, and resented the idea of painting out of necessity, or changing one's style to fit within a certain mold. As such, Tanguy's canvases are uniquely original, highly coveted, and rarely seen at auction. The provenance of this work underscores the inventive spirit and unconventional freedom at the heart of Yves Tanguy's artistic practice and, serving as an exquisite manifesto of surrealist aesthetics with great purity of execution, Bonhams is honored to platform Je tourne la tête vers moi's auction debut.

provenance: Stendahl Galleries, Los Angeles. | Private collection, San Francisco (acquired from the above on January 4, 1960). | Thence by descent to the present owner. | | Exhibited | San Francisco, San Francisco Museum of Art, Modern Masters in West Coast Collections, An Exhibition Selected in Celebration of the Twenty-Fifth Anniversary of the San Francisco Museum of Art, 1935-1960, October 18 - November 27, 1960. | | | A leading proponent of the global avant-garde and fundamental Bauhaus figure, László Moholy-Nagy's artistic output reveals a diverse practice that spans across photography, painting, sculpture, film, and design: defying all attempts at categorization. | | As Western civilization struggled to reconcile with a rapidly changing world, Moholy-Nagy's innovative artistic practice relentlessly sought to question the role of the art object and artist in society. Heavily ensconced within Bauhaus, Dada, and Constructivist theories, Moholy-Nagy believed that art should adapt with the times, reach the general masses, and reflect the ever-evolving developments in technology. Rather than demanding the amalgamation of art and technology, however, Moholy-Nagy's art encouraged viewers to analyze their perception of technology, and reconsider how the machine could best be utilized to serve the needs of humankind. The clean lines and meticulously reduced forms, now a hallmark of Moholy-Nagy's work, have always been ingrained within the artist's oeuvre and rhetoric: willing a future world of clean, advanced modernity ushered in by technological industry. | | Painted in 1939, CH9 is the ninth work in the artist's 'CH' series, aptly titled to represent the body of works created throughout the artist's time in Chicago. Forced to flee the rise of Nazi control in Europe, László Moholy-Nagy moved to the United States in 1937, eventually settling in Chicago where he opened his own design school, The New Bauhaus - American School of Design (later becoming the Institute of Design in 1944). While the artist's days in America were filled with the responsibilities of administration and teaching, Moholy-Nagy's interest in the creative potential of industrial materials, and how this potential could be harnessed across various artistic disciplines, never ceased. With the outbreak of WWII, the New Bauhaus adjusted to the wartime socioeconomic climate, resulting in an even stronger focus on functional design and the fundamental understanding of modern materials. In Moholy-Nagy's personal artistic practice, this meant incorporating industrial materials such as sheet metal. CH9 is painted canvas laid down on a panel of aluminum, a decision suggested as most likely original to the artist given how deeply the use of recycled materials was ingrained within Moholy-Nagy's aesthetic practice and ideological beliefs. Ever the innovator, and constantly developing, it has also been suggested that there may in fact be another Moholy-Nagy work on the panel, hidden beneath the canvas. | | While Moholy-Nagy's legacy is most-typically linked with the photogram and his iconic Light Prop kinetic sculptures, painting remained a visionary medium for the artist throughout his oeuvre. Walter Gropius once wrote that: "Entirely unprejudiced by conventional methods, he ventured into ever new experiments with the curiosity of a scientist" (Schlemmer, The Theater of the Bauhaus, Middletown, 1961, p. 11). Moholy-Nagy's experiments with paint resulted in dynamic worlds filled with floating, colorful possibilities that disrupted all traditional modes of seeing. In the present work, the stark contrast of the archipelago of capsular elements against the white background creates abstract patterns of light and dark, continuing an experimentation with light that was prevalent throughout the artist's career. Moholy-Nagy's passion for light as an emotive experience, aesthetic ideal, and profound philosophical study became a wholly consuming quest in the artist's life, as he sought to create not only with color and line, but light itself. Often bringing home large panes of Rhodoid, a plastic of vitreous transparency, Moholy-Nagy would paint the same abstract elements from previous paintings directly onto the plastic. As light passed through the newly painted plastic sheet, the artist reveled in comparing the two-dimensional effect of the original, painted canvas in relation to the shadows cast from the three-dimensional 'light modulator'. | | Painted on canvas as opposed to transparent sheet, CH9 seeks to extricate optimum contrasts, not only in light, but in the sensations induced from the composition's colors, spatial tensions, forms, lines, and surface texture. The sharply sketched lines of the main, bolt-like motif form an exacting 90-degree angle that is quickly offset by the rounded edges and curvilinear lines on the shape's outer edges. The delicately painted islands of stippled impasto create a tangible texture in the green capsule's lower half, while the upper half of the capsule's sparing application of paint results in a smooth finish. Though made up of disparate, contrasting formal elements, CH9's composition remains balanced, as if unified through some grandly synergetic, cosmic order. Moholy-Nagy's ability to find unity of form and mastery of contrasting tensions through paint, as seen in the present work, was one of the artist's primary reasons for continuing to experiment with the painted medium in addition to his creations of kinetic art. When writing to František Kalivoda in 1936 about his 'strange' proclivity for painting, Moholy-Nagy explained that: "I started out by rediscovering the visual fundamentals of space, color, texture, form and plasticity–open to every human being. I have always to go back to these things...to recharge my willingness to go beyond. To keep one from tearing one's nerves in all directions there must be the calm of tangible achievement–the one problem solved. For me it is abstract painting" (Moholy-Nagy quoted in J.H. Caton, The Utopian Vision of Moholy-Nagy, Ann Arbor, 1984, p. 55). For Moholy-Nagy, painting was a visionary medium; an outlet through which the artist could explore the transformative power of visual art and bolster his hopes for a better future. | | Throughout his life, László Moholy-Nagy incessantly strove to interpret space in its relation to time, a visionary artist whose imagination stretched far beyond the limits of existent conventions of seeing. His daring compositions of non-figural abstractions offered viewers a blueprint for the reconfiguration of one's perception. Moholy-Nagy emphatically believed that art could, and should, work side-by-side with technology to better humanity. As both an artist and teacher, he was convinced of art's ability to educate, and stated: "Art sharpens one's senses, one's view, one's mind and one's observations". By habituating viewers to new, modern modes of perception, Moholy-Nagy believed that art could transform the world and shape a better future. This optimistic idealism, along with his technical brilliance and abounding zeal for innovation, are palpable in the profound purity of the present work: an enduring balance of tension between movement and stasis, light and dark, opaque depth and shallow translucence. Measuring over three feet in both directions, CH9 is a both a monumental and rare example of László Moholy-Nagy's technical genius. Publicly seen seemingly only once in its lifetime and an exciting new discovery for the artist's records, Bonhams is thrilled to bring this seminal work to auction for the very first time. |

Barnett, Kandinsky, Watercolours, Catalogue Raisonné, Vol. II, 1922-1944, New York, 1994, no. 876 (illustration of the artist's sketch in the handlist p. 223). | | | For Wassily Kandinsky, art was always invention. His exacting artistic practice, particularly bolstered during his time at the Bauhaus (1922-1932) in Germany, was wholly in service of the realization of a 'science of art'. This theory, informed by psychological study and structural exactitude, was grounded in his belief that energy, movement, and rhythm enlivened one's perception of fundamental pictorial elements, thus triggering an inner resonance or spiritual vibration that could evoke an innately powerful emotional response. Lila, executed in 1928, masterfully illustrates the apogee of Kandinsky's realization of a universal order of harmony. Bold in its radiant coloring and rhythmic interplay of forms, this highly finished work on paper is a stunning exemplar of the transcendent elegance and explosive dynamism characteristic of Kandinsky's Bauhaus years. | | While Kandinsky created watercolor works throughout his career, it was only in later years that the medium began to assume a more prominent role in the artist's oeuvre. Previously used as preliminary studies considered supplemental to his paintings, it was not until his time at the Bauhaus that Kandinsky, feeling empowered to expand upon his means of expression, began to consider watercolors as individual works in their own right. From 1924 onwards, his watercolors were all assigned unique titles, no longer simply 'Entwurf zu' (Study of) or 'Projekt für' (Project for), these works now became 'Aglow' and 'Now Upwards!', giving them elevated status amongst his output. Accordingly, Kandinsky's use of the watercolor medium steadily increased throughout the decade; compared to the only twenty-five oil paintings created in 1928, he produced over a hundred watercolors, illustrating a voracious appetite for the medium. Elevated in their degrees of explicitness and elaboration, Kandinsky transcended the material limitations of oil in favor of the elusive qualities inherent in watercolor. | | The soft tonal shifts and slight gradations in coloration across the fine violet mist of the present work's compositional surface speak to Kandinsky's use of the 'Spritztechnik,' an airbrush-esque technique the artist first used in 1927 after it was introduced to him by friend and Bauhaus neighbor Paul Klee. An iconic component of his handling in many of works on paper from 1928-1930, Kandinsky's Spritztechnik created delicate transparencies that imbued his compositions with a more cosmic dimension, reflecting a newfound layer of atmospheric depth within the space as geometric elements hover and glide atop the surface. The present work's bold lilac coloring, pulsating with energy, has been understood as a distant memory of Kandinsky's Russian origins and the colors of Eastern cultures. The soft, sprayed application of modulated color in Lila collides abruptly with the precise geometric elements and boldly rendered lines: manipulating a continuous interplay between the spontaneous and the controlled. | | The present work's abstract arrangement of geometric forms is brimming with pictorial significance. Kandinsky, who believed in the expressive response evoked by the tension, contrasts, and consonance of forms, sought to create a world of heightened differentiation. It was his belief that the combination of circle and triangle created the most evocative juxtaposition, as it exemplified the power of abstract forms and their symphonic expression. He assigned profound spiritual and emotional meaning to the triangle, viewing it not merely as a geometric form, but as a visionary symbol of humanity's ascendent spiritual movement. In relation to the triangle, charged in the center of the pictorial space with connotations of significance, the present work's composition contains an extraordinary series of interactions between smaller triangles and circles, rectilinear shapes, and reverberating clusters of lines. The angular, zig-zagging lines piercing through the assemblage of circles, triangles, and curvilinear forms in Lila resemble jagged bolts of lightning – a visual link to the cosmos, symbolic of a higher order, power, and divine punishment. A carefully selected theater of opposing forces, the present work's dramatic contrasts and bold forms dominate the composition: a tour de force of Kandinsky's abstract language. | | Lila, brimming with explosive tension and a taut dynamism, presents the culmination of Kandinsky's pictorial achievement, attesting to the unique creative vision and innovative spirit of this seminal artist of the modern era. Kandinsky's faith in the power of line, color, and form is intuited through the profound lyricism of the work, fulfilling the artist's oft-stated desire for his compositions to become complete worlds in and of themselves. Through symbolism, these worlds express a newer, truer reality than is familiar to us. The individual forms, lines, and colors in Lila do not deign to have a direct association with figurative reality, but, when combined, their abstract forms are endowed with a pictorial significance that conveys an underlying energy and universal order of harmony. | | Lila was acquired by the esteemed art collector and dealer Emilie Esther Scheyer - commonly referred to by the moniker 'Galka' - shortly after its execution, in July 1928. Appearing in the opening provenance of some of the century's finest examples of European modernism, Scheyer was a tireless promoter of the genre and played an integral role in the American reception of the artist group 'The Blue Four', which comprised Lyonel Feininger, Paul Klee, Alexej von Jawlensky, and Wassily Kandinsky himself. A major factor in Scheyer's development of the group's success in the States were the travelling exhibitions that she organized, which began in the late 1920s. The present work was included in some of these opening exhibitions before ultimately being acquired by Charlotte Mack in 1931. Acquired from her by the family of the present owner and known only to Vivian Endicott Barnett from the artist's handlist illustration, Lila has not been seen in public since 1931 and comes to auction for the very first time. |

Sale, Germany. | Private collection, Germany. | Sale: Phillips de Pury & Company, New York, Contemporary Art I, May 12, 2005, Lot 45. | Private collection, US. | Acquired from the above by the present owner. | | Exhibited | Paris, Galerie Thaddaeus Ropac, Andy Warhol: The Statue of Liberty, March 6 - April 7, 1999, no. 25 (exh. cat., illustrated n.p.). | | | Painted the year before his death, Andy Warhol's Statue of Liberty marks one of the last great declarations of the master Pop artist's career. This synthetic polymer and acrylic painting is one in a larger series that captures a pivotal moment of renewal, turning his brush to one of the great American symbols in a swan song moment. An icon of American liberty and its vainglorious place amongst the global community, there are fewer images that conjure the American spirit as intensely as the visage of Lady Liberty. Warhol's rendition, emerging through an energetic script of verdigris and inky black, provides us with an unfinished monument; an examination of a national-cultural symbol. | | In the mid-1980s, Warhol had returned to creating entirely hand-painted canvases, a process reminiscent of his early years, while continuing a parallel practice of his signature silkscreen technique. His revived interest in a more manual approach coincided with a broader resurgence of gestural easel painting in the booming New York art scene. It was during that period that Swiss dealer Bruno Bischofberger initiated a high-profile collaboration between Warhol and two of the era's rising stars, Jean-Michel Basquiat and Francesco Clemente. The partnership proved especially fruitful between Warhol and Basquiat, inspiring a refreshed painterly energy in Warhol's solo production. The younger artist introduced him to the oil stick, prompting his embrace of expressive, hand-drawn elements, visible here in the loose handling of paint. | | As a former graphic artist, Warhol immediately understood the power of a distinctive visual symbol that spoke to larger cultural mores, from the Hollywood celebrity to Leonardo da Vinci's Last Supper to the dollar sign. The Statue of Liberty—which fit very well in this category—was not a new subject for Warhol. He had first explored it in 1962, basing a series of prints on a postcard image of the monument. The fact that it made a return to his oeuvre in 1986 should not be surprising, considering the statue's omnipresence in the public imagination exactly one hundred years after the statue's arrival in New York from France as a diplomatic gift. Recently restored to celebrate its centennial, new color photographs of the statue proliferated in print magazines, newspapers, and tourist memorabilia. The incessant press coverage fit perfectly with one of the artist's trademark fascinations. Warhol was deeply invested in the social effects of this kind of media saturation, particularly the way that the repeated mechanical reproduction of an image—of a person or a symbol—changes our understanding of that very subject as something degraded and disconnected from its original source. | | One such place where Lady Liberty's face appeared was on a commemorative tin of Fabis brand French cookies that inspired this painting's composition. At the lower left, Warhol painted the word "Fabis" in bubble letters, and above it, the tagline "les bons biscuits" ("the good cookies"). The American and French flags that appeared behind the logo of the souvenir tin allude to the statue's origin and remind the public of the values of freedom and democracy shared between the two nations. | | The origins of this image in such a mass culture product perfectly align with the artist's lifelong preoccupation with the rampant commercialism of twentieth century capitalist society and its connection to symbolic abstractions of American moral principles. In many ways, this late work can be seen as a bookend to his career, evoking the hand-painted process and use of a brand logo that featured in his breakthrough 1962 Ferus Gallery show of 32 Campbell's Soup Cans in Los Angeles. Warhol's choice of a greenish hue, recalling the oxidized copper of the original monument sets it apart from other versions in this series, including silkscreens in varied palettes and camouflage motifs. Other examples from this late series are held in major public collections, including The Broad in Los Angeles and The Andy Warhol Museum in Pittsburgh.

provenance: Private collection, US (acquired directly from the artist). | Acquired from the above by the present owner. | | | | Few artists have mapped the mythology of American aspiration with as much wit and profundity as Richard Prince. In Mustang Painting (2014–2016), the artist revisits one of the country's most enduring emblems of freedom and desire: the muscle car. Suspended over a saturated violet ground, the car – an iconic and rare Shelby Mustang GT350 - appears to hover between motion and stillness, its wheels dancing lightly on their tread. At once an image and an apparition, it crystallizes Prince's fascination with the promises and delusions that animate the American dream. | | Prince's career has long been entwined with the visual rhetoric of advertising and desire. Beginning in the late 1970s with his now-canonical Cowboys and Girlfriends series, he appropriated mass-media imagery to expose the coded fantasies underpinning masculinity, sexuality, and success. The muscle car entered his iconography as a natural extension of these themes: a fetish object of autonomy and performance, and a proxy for identity itself. In Mustang Painting, Prince reanimates that motif not through direct quotation from an advertisement, but through an image already mediated by the screen and the printer. The result is both painterly and mechanical, a composition whose digital inkjet underlayer is inflected with visceral streaks of acrylic paint, bridging the distance between the seductive gloss of commerce and the expressive force of painting. | | The Mustang, of course, bears its own cultural meaning. Launched in 1964 as the sports car for a newly mobile middle class, it was designed to embody youth, rebellion, and self-invention. Here, it menaces with an unnatural intensity, rendered in the synthetic hues of a dream sequence. Yellows and electric blues that dissolve into the royal violet of the background. The car is less an object than an attitude, an avatar of speed and seduction suspended in painterly limbo. | | Prince's hybrid process reflects his ongoing dialogue with the traditions of Pop. Like Warhol before him, he understands that the image is never neutral; yet unlike Warhol, Prince allows the image to reassert the hand of the artist amid the mechanics of reproduction. The inkjet transfer and Prince's overpainting blurs authorship and authenticity. | | Occupying a commanding scale that recalls the monumental proportions of roadside billboards, its single, central subject radiates an almost devotional focus. The Mustang here is not merely an icon of mid-century Americana but a mirror for the spectator's own projections of power and freedom. Prince's art has always courted this ambiguity, the fine line between critique and complicity, between desire and disillusion. | | Mustang Painting stands as a late meditation on the mirage of freedom that defines the American image world. It is a painting about velocity and stasis. Within its vivid field of color and glare, Prince distills half a century of American dreaming into a single, dazzling pause.

provenance: Galería OMR, Mexico City. | Acquired from the above by the present owner. | | | Born in 1959 in Antwerp, Belgium, Francis Alÿs departed a career in architecture to relocate to Mexico City in 1986 and begin his career as an artist. Interested in the polemics of urban spaces, geopolitical issues and social practices, Alÿs' interdisciplinary oeuvre examines these realms through the lens of poetry, fables, and imagination. Spanning actions, painting, drawing, video, and other media, Alÿs continuously challenges the boundaries of artmaking through a diverse body of work that aims to intervene in the everyday. | | Untitled (Sign Painting Project) (1996) stems from a series of paintings in which Alÿs embarked on a collaborative partnership with a number of Mexico City's commercial sign painters, or rotulistas. Most often working with Juan Garcia, Enrique Huerta and Emilio Rivera, Alÿs commissioned various rotulistas to create enlarged copies of his paintings. Wanting to make the series "more anonymous" and in an effort to reduce the value of each painting he commissioned, Alÿs established some important conditions for the work. First, there would be no limit to the number of versions that could be made for any single image. Second, versions of his paintings could be made by multiple different studios. And third, buyers could have as many versions as they wanted 'made to order.' Each artist involved would then receive equal credits and profits, making them 'collaborators' of his work (Catherine Lampert, "The Liar," Francis Alÿs: the Prophet and the Fly, pp. 17-18). | | With this conceptual structure behind the paintings, Alÿs disrupts the Renaissance models of artist studios, proposing a foil to contemporaries like Jeff Koons and Damien Hirst who famously embraced the model's commercial framework. This action would have a real-world social impact and actively support the rotulistas' profession, a career which at the time had been diminishing with the rise of reproducible printed images. Deliberately meddling with the art market, it also challenged the art industry's system for ascribing value to artworks and attempts to block its very modus operandi. | | A clear questioning of authorship, this series of paintings also proposes a profound reflection on the limits between fine art and craftsmanship, and the variable effect of different subjective viewpoints on a single image. Curator Cuauhtémoc Medina explains, "he saw the rotulistas working in the manner of an ancient scuola, sharing a common iconography and a set of social codes, as well as a 'play of translations' that transmitted 'an idea from one person to another" (quoted in "Entries," Francis Alÿs: A Story of Deception London, 2010, p. 59). The exchange is even more layered in that Alÿs' painting practice takes partial inspiration from Mexican sign painting. On the genesis for his for this work, Alÿs has said: "I was profoundly under the spell of pre-Renaissance painting during my years of university in Italy: from Lorenzetti to Fra Angelico. Even to this day, my iconography is a combination of that imagery and the language of Mexican sign painting. This blend allowed me to find a personal way of materializing images" (Carla Faesler, "Interview: Francis Alÿs," Bomb Magazine, July 1, 2011, online). | | With a multiplicity of versions available, Alÿs also here engages with an essential idea within Conceptual Art whereby the physical paintings themselves are less significant than the fundamental concepts behind the series. This is perhaps most symbolically realized by the subject of the paintings which center on familiar images and objects. There is an emphasis on the way that different artists interpret these images, which are based on the everyday but are deeply inspired by Alÿs' immersion in fairy tales and fables, Surrealism, children's books and early Italian Renaissance paintings. Each artist can take the images from Alÿs' fantasy and change their reception by way of unique approaches to the same basic concept. And different viewers can experience the same images in different ways at the same time. It is here that Alÿs' infamous poetic vocabulary takes place within the series. Curator Mark Godfrey explains that the "poetic qualities of Alÿs's projects reside in their fantastical absurdity, their transience or incompletion, their imaginative imagery, and most of all in their enigmatic openness to interpretation" (quoted in "Politics/Poetics: The Work of Francis Alÿs, Francis Alÿs: A Story of Deception, New York, 2011, p. 9). | | Alÿs considers poetry to be an essential element for political questioning and intervention, explaining that "poetic license operates like a hiatus – an 'agent provocateur'... Through the absurd and sometimes impertinent nature of the poetic act, art provokes a moment of suspended meaning, a sensation of senselessness that may reveal the absurdity of the situation... Via this act of transgression, the poetic act makes one step back for an instant from the circumstances. In short, it may make one look at things differently" (Ibid.). Always concerned with the destabilized nature of politics globally, but particularly in Latin America where he resides, Alÿs' poetic actions and paintings aim to generate perspective in the viewer that can lead to change in the real world.

provenance: Galería Garcés Velásquez, Bogotá. | Acquired from the above by the present owner. | | Exhibited | Chicago, Museum of Contemporary Art, Doris Salcedo, February 21 - May 24, 2015 (another version exhibited). | Basel, Fondation Beyeler, Doris Salcedo, May 21 - September 17, 2023 (another version exhibited) (exh. cat., illustrated pp. 63-70). | | | | Executed in 1993, Atrabiliarios is one of Doris Salcedo's most iconic early installations exploring themes that would become central to her practice including absence, violence, elegy, trauma, and healing. Taking its title from the Latin phrase atra bilis—or, the melancholy of mourning—the series consists of (mostly female) shoes placed in wall niches then covered with a thin animal fiber membrane and sewn with surgical thread. The shoes are either original or replicas of shoes that once belonged to some of the hundreds of thousands of desaparecidos (missing persons), due to violence related to Colombia's decades-long civil war, one of the longest running in the world. | | Born in Bogotá in 1958, throughout most of her life Salcedo has witnessed the far-reaching effects the ongoing conflict has had on every aspect of Colombian society. Influenced by her former mentor Beatriz González's use of common objects as well as Joseph Beuys' question of how to heal after collective social trauma, Salcedo's process often begins with a specific event for which she will spend years researching by interviewing victims of violence or their families. In speaking to those affected by atrocities relating to Colombia's civil war, Salcedo learned that shoes were one of the few means available to relatives for deciphering the identity of those found in mass graves. Though her works are often composed of simple materials—such as flowers, thread, needles, human hair, furniture, or in this case shoes—her works manage to be suggestive of people without her ever outlining a figure, further highlighting their very absence. | | "I work with materials that are already charged with significance," Salcedo has said. "Used materials are profoundly human; they all bespeak the presence of a human being" (quoted in Mary Schneider Enriquez, "Salcedo's Influences: Artists, Works, Practices," Doris Salcedo: The Materiality of Mourning, Cambridge, 2016, p. 40). With this choice of media her work is both commemorating and documenting—leaving a trace of that absence, one that is continued to be felt by victims' families through these very objects. Similar to Salcedo's Untitled series—whereby the absence of victims is evocatively conveyed by filling domestic furniture such as chairs and armoires with cement—the use of personal belongings in Atrabiliarios conjures the memory of the desaparecidos, acting as a requiem meant to impart empathy in the viewer. As the artist herself explains, "there is nothing more human than mourning; it restores humanity" (quoted in "Presenting Absence: The Work of Doris Salcedo," Doris Salcedo, Chicago 2015, p. 18). | | Though the use of pre-fabricated objects nods to the Minimalist tradition and that of the readymade, Salcedo's materials—inseparable from the affect of a human trace—represent a significant departure from the detachment provoked by mass industrial production. Salcedo then fills, covers, welds, or shatters and reconstructs these objects, creating an ephemeral, dream-like effect that renders these everyday domestic objects ultimately unusable and therefore uncanny. In Atrabiliarios, this is achieved via the semi-translucent membrane, effectively blurring the shoes from clear view. Together with its yellow tint, it mimics the effect of looking at a sepia photograph. "Critical to Salcedo's sculptures," Mary Schneider Enriquez writes, "is the idea of the uncanny... The awkward reconfiguration... results in sculptures that are at once known and unknown." (quoted in "Introduction," Doris Salcedo: The Materiality of Mourning, Cambridge, 2016, p. 5). | | Crucially, the personal stories tied to the objects never overtly make it into the works themselves. This in part is a commentary on the way that events of violence affecting large groups—especially those which occur in more marginalized geopolitical areas—are often reported without names, faces, or personal stories attached to them. Importantly, the absence of these specific, personal details also serves to remind the viewer that these struggles are universal in that they represent a life that could have been anyone's. Though this series is related to a conflict pertaining to the artist's home country, her works often concern events and peoples across the globe. Of this Salcedo has said, "my work not only comes from Colombia, it derives from turmoil and civil war—and civil war, as Hannah Arendt wrote in 1963, 'is raging all over the earth'" (Doris Salcedo, as quoted in "From the Artist," Doris Salcedo: The Materiality of Mourning, Cambridge, 2016, p. xvii). | | Instead, Salcedo takes inspiration from Holocaust survivor Paul Celan, and her work's mechanisms recall the therapeutic and healing aims of artist Lygia Clark. Like Celan—who wrote poetry while living through an unimaginable situation—Salcedo uses a resolutely poetic artistic language to create evocative sculptures about loss and human cruelty. "If mourning restores humanity, and Salcedo's sculptures create sites for mourning," curator Julie Rodrigues Widholm writes, "then she creates art that counters dehumanizing acts with humane ones. In the face of the widespread injustice and suffering that accompany systemic violence, Salcedo's work creates spaces where we can reaffirm life by confronting—seeing, hearing and acknowledging—the other. In doing so, it is both urgent and timeless." (quoted in "Presenting Absence: The Work of Doris Salcedo," Doris Salcedo, Chicago 2015, p. 19). Like Clark—who departed her Neo-concrete practice after the Brazilian dictatorship began in 1964—Salcedo's approach takes the conjecture that art, therefore, can be an effective medium for the survival and healing of the human spirit. "Art can then act in the manner of a pharmakon, a remedy" (Seloua Luste Boulbina, "Doris Salcedo's Unsubmissive Hauntology," Doris Salcedo, Basel, 2023, p. 23). | | Rarely in private hands and offered at auction, Salcedo's Atrabiliarios are held in the permanent collections of numerous prestigious institutional collections worldwide, including the Museum of Modern Art and the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum in New York; the Institute of Contemporary Art, Boston; the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art; the Los Angeles County Museum of Art; Detroit Institute of Arts; the Akron Museum of Art; the Tate Modern, London; and Moderna Museet, Stockholm, among others.
