In the lineage of Duchamp, who famously remarked that the viewer completes the work of art, Gonzalez-Torres work invites the viewer into an individualized experience with art, one in which they actively participate in his works' meanings. "Untitled" (Last Light) is a hallmark piece within one of the artist's most recognizable and captivating bodies of work, the light strings. These works can be installed in different configurations by the owner or exhibitor each time they are shown; their choices of configuration complete the work. Whenever a bulb burns out, it must be promptly replaced, perhaps instilling a potential for continual renewal that is both actual and metaphorical. (The work can also be exhibited with all the bulbs turned off.) Though the work resembles standard and widely available string lights, to experience Gonzalez-Torres' light strings is an emotive experience that can elicit a wide range of associations and interpretations. | | The first work that utilized light bulbs as a material, "Untitled" (March 5th) #2 (1991), was made the same year that Gonzalez-Torres lost his partner, Ross Laycock, to HIV/AIDS, and the parenthetical portion of this work's title references Laycock's birthday. In considering the late artist's personal memory, the utilization of light bulbs as a material could be an allusion to the practice of lighting a candle in remembrance of a lost one. Andrea Rosen, Gonzalez-Torres' longtime gallerist, has remarked on the importance of political and social theories, philosophical and psychological writings, the history of artistic and conceptual movements, as well as the artist's own experience – including his childhood in Cuba in the development of his visual index. Mentioning stories Gonzalez-Torres would recount to her of how the doorways to small stores were lined with strings of light." ('"Untitled" The Neverending Portrait', Felix Gonzalez-Torres, Ostfildern-Ruit, 1997, p. 58). Yet as memories can be nonlinear and accumulate into a palimpsest of experiences, the light string works also evoke travel and the artist's memories of spending time in Paris – the city of lights. | | Assembled from prefabricated everyday materials, the replaceability of the material in Gonzalez-Torres' work expresses an idea central to Conceptual art practices: with a devaluation of the material qualities of the work it is not the materiality of the object itself but rather the meanings behind the work which gives it value. Composed of twenty-four light bulbs, with bulbs placed at six-inch intervals, on twenty-four-foot-long cords,"Untitled" (Last Light) is one of twenty-four light string works the artist made, and one of only two examples from the series which are editioned pieces. "Untitled" (Last Light) is in an edition of twenty-four with 6 Artist Proofs. | | Numbers appear throughout Gonzalez-Torres' works; as the artist himself remarks in an interview with Tim Rollins: "I do like uncanny numbers. Things happen to me around certain numbers: 5, 24, 12... If the piece is about something that is very distant to me, then numbers like 17, 35, and 21 sound perfect because they are numbers that I would never use for anything except for a piece that is very uncomfortable" (the artist in Bill Bartman, ed., Felix Gonzalez-Torres, New York, 1993, p. 8). Despite wanting the viewer to create meaning for themselves, unlike the Minimalists Gonzalez-Torres did not deny the subjectiveness of experience as well as how the context in which a work is exhibited inevitably has an effect on the work. As the artist explains in the same interview with Tim Rollins, "Forms gather meaning from the historical moment.....But after twenty years of feminist discourse and feminist theory we have come to realize that "just looking" is not just looking but that looking is invested with identity: gender, socioeconomic status, race, sexual orientation... Looking is invested with lots of other texts"(ibid.). | | Time is a recurring theme within Gonzalez-Torres' oeuvre. Here, the twenty-four bulbs may represent each hour of the day. . This work operates similarly to his iconic 1987-1990 work, "Untitled" (Perfect Lovers) —where two identical commercial clocks are installed side by side, initially set to the same time, yet will invariably fall out of sync. In the light strings works, sooner or later a bulb will burn out which must promptly be replaced. Both of these works can function on a similar metaphorical apparatus, whereby the work could alludes to the cycle of life and death, day and night, temporality and loss, celebration and mourning. But perhaps most crucially, rebirth and renewal, as the owner or installer must actively replace any bulb that burns out. | | Like Dan Flavin, Gonzalez-Torres chose for almost all his works to be "Untitled" – specifically enclosed in quotation marks reflecting the hierarchies embedded in language, broadening the work's interpretive possibilities. Also like in Dan Flavin's work, many of Gonzalez-Torres' works (including most of the light string works ) carry a parenthetical title. In looking at the parenthetical text chosen for this piece, "Last Light" may reference twilight, suggesting that while daylight is still present the night will soon come. In this way, "Untitled" (Last Light) — which when interpreted as the nineteenth work in the series, or 7pm if one is interpreting it within the twenty-four hours in a day— may also be a reference to or acknowledgement of mortality, perhaps of oneself, a friend or loved one, or of Gonzalez-Torres. Having watched his own partner succumb to HIV/AIDS and he would also pass away due to complications relating to the disease three years later. | | Yet despite the prevalence of death, degradation, and endings in his work, they nonetheless also hold an utter optimism in the potential to make something of remaining time, and a hopefulness that exists with the possibility for rebirth. As an edition, carrying the concept of, multiplicity, perhaps "Untitled" (Last Light) also alludes to a sense of infinity, the sunrise and the sunset, or the cycle of life where life and death are infinitely connected. With this cycle, time becomes infinite again. | | As Rosen explains, "In confronting Ross' death, Felix was also confronting his own, and with the full extent of his desire for life... It is extremely clear that Felix focused on creating systems to ensure that the works did not disappear permanently... What emerges is that the work is less about the self-aggrandizing implications of immortality than the desire for the continuation of life... The idea of life lived to its fullest propelled Felix" (Ibid., p. 44). If the nature of all art is, as González-Torres believed, fundamentally political, then his political stance was to render agency back to the viewer or installer as a symbol for the agency they can take to construct meaning in their own lives or the world around them. "So, in his gentle and generous way" Rosen goes on, "Felix created structures that subtly but actively lead the viewer, and more particularly, the owner through the revelatory process of freedom of choice and possibility of influence through choice" (Ibid., p. 57). | | With seven of the twenty-four editions held in prestigious museum collections worldwide, including the Art Institute of Chicago; the Centre Pompidou in Paris; Harvard Art Museums, Cambridge; the Museum of Contemporary Art, Los Angeles; The Israel Museum, Jerusalem; the Walker Art Museum, Minneapolis and The National Museum of Art, Osaka, it is no question that "Untitled" (Last Light) is recognized as a defining work of contemporary art.

Herkenhoff, et al., Cildo Meireles, London, 1999 (illustrated p. 18). | | | "For me the art object must, despite everything else, be instantly seductive; it cannot work without that seductive involvement... If something has sufficient poetic power to be considered as an art object, it should be comprehensible to anyone, without the provision of extra information. This is why I try to make art which has that level of communication and immediacy." | - Cildo Meireles | | | Bridging Brazil's Neo-Concretist and Conceptual art practices, Cildo Meireles is one of the most respected Latin American artists of the latter half of the twentieth century. Known for his ambitious and extraordinarily diverse practice, which comprises drawing, sculpture, installation and performance via a wide array of media, Meireles sought to challenge the concepts and structures we assume and take for granted. With a philosophical and sometimes political modus operandi, his questions range from the metaphysical to the social, emphasizing themes that includes space and time, the art object, as well as economic, social and hierarchical systems and beliefs. As Brazilian curator Paulo Herkenhoff writes, "throughout the work of Cildo Meireles, there is a constant manifestation of tension and torsion––whether in the realms of aesthetics, perception, science or economics. Centering on our experience of these different branches of knowledge, his art aims to generate new meaning through recognition of the limits and fallibility of these systems of understanding." (Paulo Herkenhoff, "A Labyrinthine Ghetto: The Work of Cildo Meireles," Cildo Meireles, London, 1999, p. 38). | | Inmensa encompasses Meireles' aim of creating work that proposes reflection and questioning in the viewer both through a poetic-artistic language and an economy of means. Comprising the work is a combination of simple domestic objects, specifically five wooden tables and three wooden chairs. These everyday objects are subverted from their everyday functionality, in this transformation becoming an impractical and illogical structure. Combined, this assemblage becomes a quasi–architectural form –– heightening the arbitrary nature of the structure that could have been arranged in myriad ways. For Meireles, the use of everyday objects as material was key to achieving art which manages to interrogate many ideas at once while remaining accessible and therefore more powerful. "What interested me was the double character... one object could simultaneously engage on two levels, both within and outside an art-historical definition of the art object," Meireles says in an interview with curator Gerardo Mosquera. (Ibid., p. 13). | | Most notably, however, it is a construction in which the smallest tables and smallest chair support the largest, eliciting a poignant visual metaphor for a social structure where the working class sustains the power and weight of the ruling elite. Executed in 1982, Inmensa was created in the wake of Meireles' most political period and served as a discreet response to the dynamics of power that played out during the Brazilian military dictatorship of 1964-1985. The regime was known for its oppressive human rights abuses which included censorship, torture, and forced disappearances, and was supported by conservative sectors such as the Catholic Church and anti-communist sectors of the middle and upper classes. Many artists––including some from the famed Neo-Concretism movement, including Lygia Clark and Helio Oiticica––could not avoid making art in response to such urgency. Meireles himself has remarked on artmaking during the period, saying: "some Brazilians felt obliged to make compromising political work at that time, even if their actual artistic and intellectual interests were apolitical, as mine were" (Ibid., p.15) | | In Latin, in mensa means "over the table," while in various modern languages, it either directly signifies or is close to the word "immense." This can also be read to describe the sense of overwhelming weight these larger components subject the smaller ones to, and their corresponding significance in real world hierarchies. Though Inmensa's components are firmly constructed together and thus appear challenging to move or theoretically deconstruct, his chosen composition keeps their apparent modularity at the forefront. It is this which conjures possibility and alternative modes of thinking in the viewer, and which the work universally appealing. As curator and writer Maaretta Jaukkuri writes of Meireles' practice, "today, we know better than ever that the banality of cruelty is no local issue. There [Meireles'] works share the quality of wishing to go beyond the metaphor in order to participate in real life processes... His means of expression... are at the same time local and global, timely and untimely, and their target is a sense of commonality, the beauty and pain of being a human being both at this specific time, and in the continuum of memories and history" (M. Jaukkuri, "To be curved with the eyes," Cildo Meireles, London, 2008, p. 36).

Jenkins, Rodin and the Art of Ancient Greece, exh. cat., The British Museum, London, 2018, no. 40 (marble version illustrated on p. 105). | | | Among the pantheon of Auguste Rodin's masterpieces, Le Baiser (The Kiss) stands as one of the most celebrated icons of modern sculpture, its fame rivalled only by that of Le Penseur (The Thinker). A consummate embodiment of sensuality and emotional truth, Le Baiser captures love at its inception; an instant suspended between innocence and abandon. The work's timeless appeal lies in its duality: at once tender and erotic, idealized and modern, it crystallizes Rodin's unrivalled ability to sculpt passion in motion. | | The story that inspired this immortal embrace originates in Canto V of Dante Alighieri's Inferno (c. 1321), which recounts the tragic tale of Francesca da Rimini and her husband's brother, Paolo Malatesta. While reading the romance of Guinevere and Lancelot together, the pair realize their own forbidden love; their first kiss, born of literary temptation, seals their fate. Discovered by Francesca's husband Gianciotto, they are murdered mid-embrace and condemned to the second circle of Hell, reserved for sins of the flesh. It was this fatal union—where passion and damnation meet—that first stirred Rodin's imagination. | | Rodin initially conceived Le Baiser as part of La Porte de l'Enfer (The Gates of Hell), the monumental bronze portal commissioned by the French government in 1880 as a sculptural interpretation of Dante's Inferno. The lovers appeared on the lower left panel of Rodin's third and final terracotta maquette, described by critic Octave Mirbeau in La France (1885). Modelled in the round and later attached to the plaster panels, their embrace was, however, deemed too tender for the cataclysmic drama of La Porte. Around 1887 Rodin removed them, replacing the group with a more tormented version, Paolo et Francesca. Yet rather than abandon the figures, he recognized their independent power and developed the composition into a freestanding sculpture—exhibited in plaster at the Brussels Salon of 1887 and later that year in bronze at Galerie Georges Petit, Paris—under the title Le Baiser. | | The original Le Baiser measured approximately 85 centimeters in height, but following its critical success in Brussels and Paris, the French state commissioned a monumental marble version in 1888, enlarged to roughly 190 centimeters. Rodin labored on this marble for a decade; unveiled at the Paris Salon of 1898, it caused a sensation. Viewers were captivated, even shocked, by the idealization and sensuality of the intertwined nudes. As contemporary critics observed, the sculpture's frank eroticism and palpable humanity signalled a break from classical restraint. Romantic love and sexuality—central to Rodin's oeuvre—were here presented without moral filter, elevated instead to the realm of the eternal. | | While Le Baiser shares thematic kinship with Rodin's other explorations of the embrace, such as L'Éternel Idole and L'Éternel Printemps, no other work so perfectly captures the dawning of desire. In Dante's text, Paolo initiates the kiss; in Rodin's re-imagining, Francesca rises toward him, her body alive with agency and anticipation. Her right leg drapes over his, a gesture of confident surrender, as she draws his head gently toward her own. Paolo, by contrast, hesitates, his left hand still cradling the book that has slipped open upon his knee, the page bent beneath the weight of their union. His other hand rests delicately upon Francesca's thigh, the fingertips expressing both passion and restraint. Their lips barely touch; the moment is one heartbeat before consummation, frozen forever at the precipice of love. | | Art historian Albert Elsen observed, "The whole impression ... is one of Paolo's slowly eroding resolve and awakening desire" (A. Elsen, Rodin's Art, Oxford, 2003, p. 211). Indeed, Rodin achieves here what few sculptors before him dared: the rendering of psychological and physical awakening in marble and bronze. Every curve and surface radiates emotion; flesh breathes, stone trembles. | | In 1898, to meet the mounting demand from collectors worldwide, Rodin authorized the celebrated Barbédienne foundry to produce bronze editions of Le Baiser in four reductions, 25 cm, 38 cm, 60 cm and 73 cm, retaining for himself the right to cast the full-scale version. The present example, cast between circa 1914 and 1918 by Gustave Leblanc-Barbédienne, belongs to the second reduction, the larger of the two 60 cm domestic-scale casts. This size, with its commanding yet intimate presence, is widely considered the most balanced and harmonious of the reductions, preserving the expressive force of the original while allowing it to inhabit the refined spaces of the modern interior. | | The bronze's surface, softly modelled and alive with Rodin's tactile energy, invites the viewer's gaze to linger. Light glides across the forms as if caressing skin, animating every subtle shift of muscle and curve. The composition's modernity lies not only in its realism but in its psychological immediacy: Rodin transforms myth into human truth, passion into permanence. | | When Le Baiser first appeared in marble, critics' responses oscillated between awe and scandal. To some, the lovers' nakedness seemed audacious; to others, it revealed a new ideal of beauty freed from academic constraint. In this tension, between propriety and passion, Rodin's genius resides. As with Antonio Canova's Psyche Revived by Cupid's Kiss (1787-1793) - held in the Louvre museum since 1824 - which had enchanted early-nineteenth-century audiences, Le Baiser reignited the Romantic fascination with love's divine folly. Yet where Canova offered mythic idealisation, Rodin presented carnal truth. His lovers are not gods but mortals, their joy and doom inseparable, their kiss both sacred and profane. | | Originally conceived as a tragedy within The Gates of Hell, the scene might once have been read as a warning against desire; an allegory of impulsive sin. Yet Rodin's reimagining transforms the narrative entirely. By extracting Paolo and Francesca from the infernal context and enlarging their moment of passion into a self-contained work, he suspends judgment itself. The lovers are no longer punished; they are redeemed through the eternalization of their love. Rodin solidifies not their doom but their joy, capturing a rapture that transcends consequence. | | Today, Le Baiser endures as an emblem of Romantic love, of beauty, resilience, and hope. The 60 cm second reduction encapsulates the essence of Rodin's achievement: a sculpture at once monumental in spirit and intimate in scale, capable of expressing universal desire within a domestic setting. In its presence, time seems to halt; the lovers remain forever poised at the brink of union, untouched by the tragedy that awaits them beyond the moment. | | Through Le Baiser, Rodin distilled the very essence of passion: raw yet refined, temporal yet eternal. It is a triumph of modernity and emotion, where love, unburdened by fate, exists purely for itself: an eternal present in bronze.

Before painting, when I talk to the person, they unconsciously assume their most characteristic pose, which in a way involves all their character and social standing - what the world has done to them and their retaliation." | – Alice Neel | | | Executed in 1930, Fanya is a powerful and intimate early portrait by Alice Neel and notably one of the earliest canvas portraits by the artist ever to appear at auction. The painting depicts Fanya Foss, a close friend of Neel's and a figure who would go on to have a celebrated career as a Hollywood screenwriter active between the 1940s and 1960s. The two women met in 1927, when Neel had just arrived in the city after her studies at the Philadelphia School of Design for Women. Searching for stability, Neel took a job at Foss's Greenwich Village bookstore, and their bond soon became an important part of the artist's early New York life. Their friendship was one of mutual admiration and intellectual exchange. Foss, a politically engaged writer with literary ambitions, encouraged Neel's growing sense of artistic and feminist independence. "Foss typified the intellectuals to whom Neel was attracted...In her two portraits of Foss, Neel expresses both admiration and annoyance...In the painting, her friend poses in a demure, unassuming manner" (C. Carr, Alice Neel: Woman, New York, 2002, p. 6). | | The sitter's composed yet emotionally charged presence is emblematic of Neel's extraordinary ability to fuse psychological depth with painterly directness. Foss sits in a soft lounge chair, an elemental motif that recurs throughout her oeuvre, functioning as both a stage and a silent witness to the lives she portrayed. Underscoring the formal and symbolic importance of this device within her practice, the chair serves as not merely a seat but a psychological anchor - a space of containment and endurance. Its iconography would follow Neel throughout her career, culminating decades later in Dr. Finger's Waiting Room, the empty chair painting that now holds her auction record, | | The year 1930 was one of profound personal crisis for Neel as it was the year her husband, Cuban painter Carlos Enríquez, left for Havana with their young daughter. This loss marked Neel deeply and that summer she threw herself into painting before suffering a devastating mental breakdown leading to a period of hospitalization. The emotional weight of this moment; grief, abandonment, and inner turmoil is palpable in Fanya. The sitter's distant, almost guarded gaze and the quiet tension of her pose mirror the artist's own psychological state during this pivotal year. Her teal dress forms a rhythmic cascade of curves that contrasts with the strength of her posture while the gesture of her hands conveys both composure and unease. The sorrow and dislocation of that period seep into Fanya in her quiet restraint, the melancholy color palette, and the air of suspension all seem to mirror the artist's own fragile state of mind. "Fanya in 1930 holds a slim hand against her chest and stares at the viewer, as if to say, 'Why am I myself? And why do you look at me?' Repose and denial of the sitter: Fanya will next say, 'No, you don't mean 'me.' I am not entirely or only myself.' And yet notice how regally – with what sublime sufferance -- she permits the viewer to doom her to portraitures apparatus" (W. Koestenbaum, Alice Neel: Paintings from the Thirties, Robert Miller 1997, p. 3). | | Fanya Foss would remain a resonant figure in Neel's imagination. She reappears in The Intellectual (1930), a related work on paper that was featured in the recent traveling retrospective organized by The Metropolitan Museum of Art in 2021, underscoring the significance of this early subject in Neel's portraiture. Together, these two works encapsulate Neel's fascination with women of intellect and conviction who, like herself, challenged the confines of gender and social expectation. Fanya not only captures a formative friendship but also embodies the raw, searching quality that defined Neel's most affecting works. | | With emotional depth, compositional clarity, and profound biographical resonance, Fanya stands as a landmark in Neel's early development, offering a deeply personal window into Neel's artistic and emotional landscape at a critical juncture in her life. It reveals the artist at a moment of personal upheaval yet remarkable creative clarity, transforming private struggle into enduring her practice- a powerful precursor to the fearless, incisive portraiture that would cement her place as one of the most important American painters of the 20th century.

Born in South Carolina, Tucker was a celebrated and deeply respected psychologist. A trailblazer in her field with countless professional accomplishments, Tucker was also a staunch supporter of the Civil Rights and Women's movements. Amongst her many notable accolades, including holding two Ph.Ds. (one in Education and one in Professional Psychology) Tucker served as the commissioner of several city departments and was the president of the California Psychology Association. Moreover, she helped found the Los Angeles Black Women's Forum and was on the board of the Westside Women's Clinic. Tucker was an active, passionate, and beloved contributor to her community, much like Ernie Barnes who was a close friend of hers. | | The present work portrays an intimate moment that is both grand and quiet. The house in the background, an iconic motif of Barnes' most successful basketball paintings, pays homage to his upbringing in North Carolina. With the figure suspended in midair, Barnes astutely and poetically articulates the full spectrum of athletic greatness wherein the journey to success is just as beautiful as the success achieved.

Sollins, Art: 21: Art in the Twenty-First Century 3, New York, 2005 (illustrated pp. 108-109). | | | | Painted in 2002-2003, Susan Rothenberg's Mares and Foals stands as a poignant synthesis of the artist's lifelong engagement with movement, gesture, and form, reimagining the iconic horse motif that defined her early career through the contemplative lens of her later years in New Mexico. | | Rothenberg's horse paintings, created primarily during the 1970s and 1980s, marked a decisive moment in the evolution of postwar American painting. At a time when minimalism and pure abstraction prevailed, Rothenberg reintroduced the figure - specifically, the horse - as a vehicle for exploring the relationship between image, gesture, and form. Rendered in a simple palette and characterized by rough, expressive brushwork, these monumental compositions balance the formal concerns of abstraction with the immediacy of figuration. The horse, abstracted and removed from narrative context, functions less as a literal subject than as an emblem of energy and presence - an exploration of motion through the medium of paint. By combining material intensity with symbolic depth, Rothenberg brought new vitality to painting, uniting the clarity of conceptual art with the emotional force of expressive gesture. Mares and Foals revisits the iconic imagery that established Rothenberg's reputation, recontextualizing it within the landscape and rhythms of her later life in New Mexico. | | In the early 1990s, Susan Rothenberg relocated from New York to a ranch in Galisteo, New Mexico, marking a new chapter in both her life and artistic practice. "It felt like a completely different situation—the light, the space of the landscape. Everything was different. It seemed like I needed to make a new start," she later reflected (quoted in M. Auping, Susan Rothenberg: Moving In Place, Fort Worth, 2009, p. 19). Although several aspects of her work evolved - most notably her expanded use of color and the integration of human figures into her works - the fundamental character of her paintings remained. Life in New Mexico merged the restlessness of Rothenberg's inner world with the unpredictability of rural experience, particularly the spirited behavior of the animals surrounding her studio. This environment inspired an extended series of works depicting rabbits, horses, dogs, goats, and snakes. The dynamic, rotating spatial compositions she had long cultivated proved ideally suited to portraying scenes of movement and interaction among multiple figures. | | Rothenberg's years in New Mexico revitalized her artistic practice, prompting her to once again draw on her enduring ability to challenge and expand painterly conventions through her distinctive approach to pictorial space and her nuanced exploration of light, color, form, and movement. Mares and Foals, which portrays a tender moment between mother and child, revisits the bold color and monumental scale of her early horse paintings, filtered through a more introspective and personal lens. The work reflects on the fragility of life, serving as a meditation on memory, stillness, and the threshold between worlds. | | "It was important that I was painting something that was alive. I didn't want to paint something inanimate. It needed to have flesh and spirit. I guess I wanted to paint the kind of energy you find in the real world rather than the abstract world" (quoted in Ibid., p. 13).

Wiener, Walton Ford: Pancha Tantra, Cologne, 2015 (illustrated pp. 76-77). | | | | Celebrated for his timeless and elegant draftsmanship, Walton Ford's Chingado is a provocative and monumental watercolor that blurs the lines between realism and fantasy, past and present, beauty and violence. Ford is a contemporary master of the natural history painting genre, drawing on traditional animal subjects in allegorical dramas to reveal the impact of humans and globalization on the natural world. Widely exhibited and often cited, Chingado is a quintessential example of Ford's compelling subversion of the visual language of natural history painting. | | Ten years after its creation, Ford described the Chingado as a disturbed scene from the imagination of a "delirious Audubon...or Akeley" (quoted in F. Hirsch, 'King of the Beasts [Walton Ford]', Art in America, Volume 96, Issue 9, October 2008). In the early 1990s, he began incorporating the imagery of nineteenth-century naturalists John James Audubon and Carl Akeley, whose paintings and dioramas remain important sources of inspiration. Ford skillfully leverages the life-size scale, lush landscapes, and meticulous details of the natural history painting genre, appropriating its visual appeal with a critical eye that reveals its layered historical and intellectual context. | | It is evident in his naturalistic treatment of animals and dynamic compositional framing that Ford pulls from an array of art historical references from the Old Masters to French Romanticism, channeling classical scenes of warfare or hunting such as Sir Peter Paul Rubens' The Tiger Hunt. One among a series of hunting scenes Rubens painted between 1614-1616, this work depicts a vicious power struggle between man and beast in a swirling storm of chaos. | | Ford distills Rubens' complex web of focal lines down to the two key visual elements of Chingado in a compelling energetic arrangement. In Rubens' example, the composition explodes in all directions with animal and human limbs bisecting each other. The tiger overtakes a defenseless man on horseback, its claws and powerful jaws sinking into the man's flesh, while shielding a tigress and her young cubs. In a strikingly similar pose, Ford's jaguar clamps its jaws around the bull's jugular, drawing ruby droplets of blood with its claws. The visual and thematic resonance between these works underscore the eternal and cyclical nature of the conflicts that lie at the bedrock of humanity: man versus man, man versus earth, and man versus beast. | | The work's title translates to fucked in common Mexican vernacular. A contemporary spin on a painting overflowing with historical flare, Ford weaves a complex web of meaning into the present work, illustrating the furious wresting of power from the jaguar, indigenous to the American continent, by the bull imported by Spanish conquistadors. "They're coupling to create Mexico," Ford later reflected (quoted in C. Tomkins, "Man and Beast: The Narrative Art of Walton Ford", The New Yorker, January 2009). | | A complex interrogation of Mexico's founding myths, Chingado excavates layers of conflict between Spanish settlers and Indigenous peoples, collapsing time in this striking metaphor. Through calligraphic texts interspersed in the margins, Ford explicitly asserts continuity between the historical Spanish Conquest of Tenochtitlan and the contemporary Zapatista rebellion in Chiapas. Other stylized inscriptions exemplify Ford's impressive use of diverse sources and sardonic political humor to articulate analogies between the past and present. Passages from the Popol Vuh, the sacred cosmological epic of the Kʼicheʼ Maya people, trace the origins of man. Mayan glyphs correspond to cycles of life and warfare, the latter of which is branded on the bull's flank. An excerpt from historian Enrique Krauze's introduction to Mexico: Biography of Power (1996) conveys the intent behind this perverse allegory: | | It is the beginning of a long history | I undertake to relate to you. | Register it all of you, and let your memory | never permit it to be forgotten. | | Chingado is not only a technical masterpiece of Ford's impressive use of watercolor, but a multilayered and rigorous investigation of colonialism, neoimperialism, and environmental devastation. It encapsulates the artist's breadth of historical knowledge, sharp critical eye, and strength in allegory, reflecting a defining moment in his career when these values came into focus to form the foundation of his ongoing practice. The present lot was included in Ford's Tigers of Wrath: Watercolors by Walton Ford, a midcareer survey presented in 2006 at the Brooklyn Museum, New York and Bestiarium at the Hamburger Bahnhof–Museum für Gegenwart, Berlin in 2010, the artist's first institutional exhibition in Europe. More recently, the Morgan Library & Museum in New York held an exhibition in 2024 in celebration of the artist's gift of 63 sketches and studies to the museum, displayed alongside larger-scale watercolors and selection of works hand-picked by the artist from the permanent collection including prints and drawings by Rembrandt, Dorothea Maria Gsell, Eugène Delacroix, Antoine-Louis Barye, and John James Audubon.

Only in that interminable and abysmal madness was Alice able to find herself." | - Roberto Fabelo | | | Born in 1950 in Camagüey, Cuba, Roberto Fabelo was a young child when the Cuban Revolution would profoundly change the trajectory of his home country through the remainder of the twentieth and twenty-first century. He would grow up as the new Republic of Cuba established itself, watching its continuous evolution in the decades since. During the same period, Fabelo has created a beguiling body of work—one of the most distinguished in Latin America for its unique approach to allegorical painting. Combining surrealism, magical realism, and Old Master techniques from art history, Fabelo's work incorporates visions and dreams that propel a deeper understanding of the complexities of the Cuban reality and the resilience of its people. | | One of Fabelo's most seminal and iconic works, Sueño de navegante portrays a large saucepot overflowing with the bodies of merpeople, contorted in various positions and within claustrophobic proximity to one another. The scene is set against a pitch-black background from which it emerges—creating the effect of a dreamscape or nightmare. Taking cues from the likes of Dürer, Goya, Rembrandt, Bosch, and Daumier, as well as literary influences like Kafka, Poe, and García Márquez, Fabelo utilizes fantasy and expression as a tool to see reality more deeply, incorporating the inner human psyche through subconscious emotions, thoughts, and associations as a way of arriving at truth. | | Incorporating many of Fabelo's most important motifs, such as the saucepot, shell-hats, and half-human creatures, the symbols in Sueño de navegante together express both horror and beauty, violence and elegance, as well as lyricism and asphyxiation. The saucepot, which frequently recurs in his oeuvre, here functions as a synecdoche for food and an allusion to the recycling of materials that characterizes Cuban daily life as a means for survival. In the artist's own words, "all Cubans are innate recyclers... It is something inherent to us as survivors of shortages and having to give up many things; recycling is a term that refers not only to material objects but also to our best sentiments—our memories, our culture. We have all had to recycle, and I've found myself in that tide, too" (Estrella Díaz, "Roberto Fabelo: 'I love even this island's trash'," On Cuba News, February 12, 2015, online). | | In Sueño de navegante, which translates to "dream of the navigator," the saucepot seems to mirror a ship, a connection heightened by the fusion of these beings to the sea in his illustration of them as merpeople. A significant motif in Fabelo's practice, water itself is absent but strongly suggested here. Nodding to Cuba's isolation, both geographically as an island and politically by way of the decades-long Castro regime. In depicting merpeople, Fabelo is making a statement about the inalienable connection of the Cuban people with water, recognizing the history of refugees who escaped on treacherous journeys by boat to pursue other lands and opportunities. Moreover, the saucepot and the fantastical figures become a stand-in for the dehumanization of the Cuban people consumed by the regime. Richly layered with meaning, Sueño de navegante illustrates Fabelo's painterly mastery, creating new worlds that serve as allegories for survival, enmeshing harsh reality with dreams, joy with pain to build a narrative that is subversively emotive as it is urgent.
